prose_changes.old: This covers Ottoman Orthodoxy's second act: the Synod of Jerusalem under Dositheus in 1672, the East's own answer to the Council of Trent; the century that produced the largest number of neomartyrs; the rise of Phanariot influence; and the abolition of the Serbian patriarchate of Peć in 1766 and the archbishopric of Ohrid in 1767. The Serbian Great Migration of 1690 placed the Karlovci church outside the Ottoman millet system from that date. The story ends with Patriarch Gregory V hanged at the Patriarchate's gate at Easter 1821.
prose_changes.new: This is the second act of Orthodoxy under Ottoman rule. In 1672 the Synod of Jerusalem, led by Patriarch Dositheus, answered French Calvinists. They had claimed that the Eastern Church shared their faith. Its confession was the East's own statement of faith, to set beside those of the West. This century also saw the most neomartyrs, and the rise of the Phanariot families. In 1766 Constantinople did away with the Serbian patriarchate of Peć. A year later it did the same to the archbishopric of Ohrid. After the Great Migration of the Serbs in 1690, their church at Karlovci lay outside the Ottoman millet system. The story ends at Easter 1821, when Patriarch Gregory V was hanged at his own gate.
prose_changes.reason: 'The East's own answer to the Council of Trent' misstated what the synod answered: its acts say it met 'against the Calvinists', prompted by French Calvinists' claims (Dositheus, Robertson 1899, lines 332-338, 457-460). It never addresses Trent. The comparison with Western confessions is kept, as the longDescription already makes it. 'Second act' now reads in plain words. Every other fact kept. Whole field rewritten.

prose_changes.old: The arrangement kept Orthodox Christianity intact through centuries of Muslim rule, at the price of tying the church to a foreign state and of Greek ecclesiastical dominance over Slavs and Arabs. A resentment that shaped every Balkan church that came after. When the empire's Christian provinces became nations in the nineteenth century, each took its own church with it, and the pattern of national Orthodox churches that exists today is the direct result. Gregory V's gate at the Phanar has never been opened since 1821: it is welded shut and painted black, and the patriarchate is still there behind it.
prose_changes.new: The arrangement kept Orthodox Christianity intact through centuries of Muslim rule. The price was a church tied to a foreign state, with Greek church leaders ruling over Slavs and Arabs. That rule bred resentment. In 1762 the Bulgarian monk Paisii of Hilendar wrote that his people suffered much wrong from Greek bishops. When the empire's Christian provinces became nations in the nineteenth century, each took its own church with it. Today's pattern of national Orthodox churches grew out of that break-up. Gregory V's gate at the Phanar has never been opened since 1821. It is welded shut and painted black, and the patriarchate is still there behind it.
prose_changes.reason: 'A resentment that shaped every Balkan church that came after' was a fragment and an unsupported sweep. It is replaced by one attested case: Paisii of Hilendar, Istoriia slavianobolgarskaia (1762), lines 6883-6884 ('много насишш неправ-Ьдно . с5 грчески владицп', much unjust violence from Greek bishops), and his complaint of 'гръцка архиерейска власть' quoted by his editor at lines 1046-1047. 'The direct result' is softened to 'grew out of'; the break-up itself is the era-9 entry's own subject. Whole field rewritten.

prose_changes.old: At Athanasius III's death the Damascus party elects the pro-Roman Cyril VI Tanas (1724); Constantinople consecrates Sylvester instead; the Antiochian patriarchate splits permanently and the Melkite Greek Catholic communion - alive today - begins; kin-shape to the Union of Brest and the Maronite union, both seated; the Orthodox side of the split continues within the later history of Ottoman-era Orthodoxy.
prose_changes.new: When Patriarch Athanasius III died in 1724, the party at Damascus chose Cyril VI Tanas, who favored union with Rome. Constantinople consecrated a rival, Sylvester, instead. The see of Antioch split for good, and the Melkite Greek Catholic Church began. It is still alive today. The split took a shape seen before, in the Union of Brest and in the Maronites' union with Rome. The Orthodox side of the split stayed part of Orthodoxy under the Ottomans.
prose_changes.reason: 'Kin-shape ... both seated' was cataloguing language ('seated' means 'has an entry'). It now says plainly that the split followed an earlier pattern; no link is claimed, since neither Brest nor the Maronites is shown to have shaped the 1724 events. 'Continues within the later history of Ottoman-era Orthodoxy' is restated plainly. Whole field rewritten.

prose_changes.old: Both churches are alive. The Melkite Greek Catholic Church has a patriarch of Antioch today, is present across the Middle East and in a large diaspora in the Americas, Europe and Australia, and worships in Arabic in the Byzantine rite while in communion with Rome. The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch continues alongside it. The split also fixed a pattern that recurs across the Christian East — an Eastern-rite church in union with Rome standing beside its Orthodox mother church, with all the ordinary difficulty that creates. Through Aleppo's presses and schools, the Melkites became significant carriers of Arabic Christian literature.
prose_changes.new: Both churches are alive. The Melkite Greek Catholic Church has a patriarch of Antioch today. It is found across the Middle East and in large communities abroad, in the Americas, Europe and Australia. It worships in Arabic in the Byzantine rite, in communion with Rome. The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch lives on beside it. The split gave the Christian East one more case of a familiar pattern. An Eastern-rite church in union with Rome stands beside the Orthodox church it came from, with all the everyday strain that brings. Through Aleppo's presses and schools, the Melkites became major carriers of Arabic Christian writing.
prose_changes.reason: 'The split also fixed a pattern' claimed the 1724 split set a pattern that the Union of Brest (1596) and the Maronite union had already set; the entry's own summary calls those earlier. Now 'one more case of a familiar pattern'. Every other fact kept. Whole field rewritten.

prose_changes.old: This is a living church and a very large one. The Philippines has one of the largest Catholic populations in the world, and the devotional culture of these centuries is still recognizably what is practiced — the pasyon chanted through Holy Week, the town fiesta for the patron saint, the processions. The unresolved question of the period, whether Filipino priests could run Filipino parishes, produced the executions of the three priests remembered as Gomburza in 1872 and fed directly into the national revolution and into the independent Philippine church that broke from Rome in 1902. The friar churches themselves survive: four of them, San Agustín in Manila among them, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
prose_changes.new: This is a living church and a very large one. The Philippines has one of the largest Catholic populations in the world. Its devotions are still much as they were in these centuries: the pasyon chanted through Holy Week, the town fiesta for the patron saint, the processions. The period left one question open: could Filipino priests run Filipino parishes? Writing in 1899, a Filipino scholar traced that quarrel to the execution of three priests in 1872. They are remembered as Gomburza. The quarrel is also often tied to the national revolution. It is tied as well to the independent Philippine church that broke from Rome in 1902. The friar churches still stand. Four of them, San Agustín in Manila among them, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
prose_changes.reason: The tie from the clergy question to Gomburza now rests on Pardo de Tavera's 1899 notes (Blair and Robertson v50, lines 8412-8413, 8441-8444). 'Fed directly into the national revolution and into the independent Philippine church' has no vendored source and is qualified as a common reading. Every other fact kept. Whole field rewritten.

escalations: Census structure (portfolio-level, for Mark): the Armenian Apostolic Church from 1650 to 1815 has no entry. The census routes the Armenian lane through 'Armenian Christianity — the Mekhitarists and the Catholic Patriarchate' (New Julfa continues into it, and it continues into the Zartonk), yet that entry's own text treats the Apostolic Church as the other, larger body. A 'continued as' link from New Julfa or into the Zartonk would claim the Catholic and Mekhitarist story is the same community as the Apostolic Church. I drafted neither; the Zartonk tie is drafted only as 'influenced'. Mekhitar did come out of the Apostolic Church: Nurikhan has him go to Etchmiadzin with the Catholicos's delegate in 1692 (lines 2866-2868). Options: (a) add an era-8 Apostolic Church entry; (b) widen this entry's scope and text; (c) keep the structure and accept 'continued as' links across the lane. Recommendation: (a).

Not a stop, for the merge: two fragments outside my change scope stay in the Philippine longDescription ('Which became the great grievance of the century that followed.') and the Armenian longDescription ('To gather, edit and print the Armenian inheritance for a people scattered across empires.'). Neither carries a relationship claim, so I did not rewrite those fields. The Philippine entry's name, 'Era-8 Segment', is cataloguing language in a public name. All sixteen fields score below the reading target; I rewrote only the five that needed a relationship fix.
